```text
Peak Poker Performance

   This also relates to the loss aversion research I discussed earlier. Be-
cause of our loss-averse brain, many players feel a strong urge to book a
small win. After all, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush as the say-
ing goes. It is for this reason that you might feel “fatigued” when you are
up. In other words, it could be a psychosomatic response. Now the oppo-
site happens when we are losing. Often we will play on and chase those
losses, even if the game is not especially good. It is painful to lose. Plus,
we often have adrenaline and cortisol rushing through our veins thanks to
the stress of losing; these two neurochemicals are stimulants, which
cause you to feel alert and awake.
   I encourage you to take the time to assess your sessions to see if loss
aversion is affecting you. If you are winning and it is a good game, and if
you are clear headed and focused, you should stay in the game. If the
game is not good, or if you are playing poorly, you should leave. Make
your decisions based on the flow of the game and not based off thoughts
and feelings driven by loss aversion.
```

```text
                                                  Readers’ Questions

   might stick with it for longer. By doing your goal behavior

♠ Think about your reason for doing these activities. It’s hard to get
   motivated if you don’t have a good reason for doing something.
   What’s your “why” for getting better? We often put off things we
   don’t really value, so think about why getting good at poker is
   important to you.
♠ Set goals. Well set goals fuel motivation. Humans are teleological
   beings: we thrive when we have a target that we are aiming at.
   Make sure your goals are specific. How many videos or hand
   reviews do you want to complete each week?
♠ Schedule hand reviews. Do them as soon as you can in the day.
   Getting them done before you get caught up in other things is
   important. Also, I recommend that my clients use something called a
   Pomodoro technique. This is where you set a timer for a certain
   amount of time (usually 20–45 minutes), and you fully focus on your
   task for that entire time with no distractions. When your time is up,
   you get to take a 10 minute break. Rinse and repeat as needed.
♠ Recognize that feelings follow behavior. We often think we need
   to “feel like it” to take action, but research shows that if we just
   get started, motivation often follows along. Besides that, our
   behavior is controllable in a way that our feelings are not. In his
   book Constructive Living, David K. Reynolds says that “the mature
   human being goes about what needs to be done regardless of
   whether that person feels great or terrible.” Having that level of
   self-control brings satisfaction and confidence.
♠ Get rest. The number one reason people give for procrastinating is
   being too tired, so make sure you are getting plenty of rest. Have
   rest and recovery built into your schedule and discipline yourself
   to make sure you get enough sleep.
```

```text
Q7) Key Psychological Factors
      What are, in your opinion, the psychological aspects that help
      the most for a person who wants to play at their highest level
      of ability?
                                                                       Daniel

   There are many factors that can help someone play at the highest level
they are capable of, and having a learner’s mindset is very important. If
you have a learner’s mindset, you will view every hand and every playing
session as a little experiment that gives you data. You want to look at this
data to see if there was anything that you could have done better or dif-
ferent. If you played very well, give yourself a little pat on the back to im-
print it on your mind. If you see things that are not to your liking, don’t
get upset or self-critical. Just make a note about what needs work. Be
curious, but not furious! The most important thing is to be honest with
yourself about what parts of your game (mental and strategic) need work
and then make a plan to address those issues. The best players are con-
stantly working to improve their games.
   One of the best things you can do is keep a daily performance journal.
This is an extremely useful tool for measuring how well you are perform-
ing and how much progress you are making towards achieving your goals.
After each playing session, write out the answers to these five questions:

   ♠ What did I do well today?
   ♠ What did I do poorly?
   ♠ What will I do differently next time?
   ♠ What lessons did I learn?
   ♠ What is my goal (or game plan) for tomorrow?

   Every session needs an evaluation because what we measure and track
determines how fast and far we will grow. Everything should be looked at
```

```text
                                                       Readers’ Questions

as data with the goal of getting a little better from each session. Always
be thinking about what you could do to get just a little bit better and then

level.
   From a psychological traits perspective, there are several traits that
are very important for poker success:

   ♠ self-discipline: impulse control is everything
   ♠ self-awareness: the basis of all improvements
   ♠ resilience: the ability to bounce back from adversity
   ♠ a growth mindset: welcome challenges with open arms because
       you know that you have what it takes to master whatever comes
       your way
   ♠ passion: a true love for the game to keep you going
   ♠ conscientiousness: diligent, consistent action as the key to
       success.


  Playing poker at your highest level of ability takes a great deal of effort
and energy. Do whatever you can to increase those two factors and you
have a good shot at succeeding.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

    Decide what you want to be good at. Is it tournaments or cash? Is it
full ring or something else? Is it a certain variant of poker? Keller and Pa-
pasan discuss the importance of dedicating yourself to your one thing in
their book The One Thing (2013). They argue that it is not possible to try
to focus on multiple things at once if you want to become really good at
something. You have to commit to whatever your one thing is going to
be. Once you know this, you can then determine what you need to study
in order to improve. After you decide on your one thing, you need to start
lining up your dominoes. In what order do you need to tackle things?
What needs to happen sequentially for you to achieve your outcomes?
    Progress is often slow, which is fine because trying to do too much at
once can be overwhelming. Break your overall goal down into smaller
chunks, and do some work towards them each day. What is one small
thing you can do today to make progress towards your goals? How can
you become 1% better? Focus on incremental gains and your results will
come sooner than you can imagine. Marginal gains over a long period of
time lead to extraordinary gains.
    The most important thing is to make progress. Don’t just get hung up
on the end result, as focusing too much on the end result might discour-
age you. As long as you set a priority for each day and meet it, you are
good to go.
    Along the way, there are likely to be obstacles. Think about what these
might be and make a plan to deal with them. Know what your personal
kryptonite is and figure out how to deactivate it. Approach your goals
with a learning mindset. Everything you do is just a little experiment and if
it doesn’t work out use the data to improve your process and get better.
Judge yourself on your efforts and not on the outcomes (especially if the
outcomes are not under your control). Keep this mindset and keep build-
ing momentum and you’ll be just fine!
```

```text
Q9) Switching Gears
      I have a habit of putting myself in great positions in tourna-
      ments and then in three hands losing it all. Most notably at
      last year’s WSOP Main Event, I was the chip leader on Day 4
      with nearly $1m more in chips than the next player. Other
      players I know have been critical of my performance asking
      “Why didn’t you just stop playing and go back to your room?”
      While I don’t think that would have been the best strategy, I
      do believe that I should have probably shifted gears. When to
      shift gears is debatable depending on your goals. The question
      I pose to you is: “How do you make yourself switch gears?”
                                                                       Mike

   From a psychological point of view the most important thing to work
on is your mindfulness. You want to be attending to the present moment
with a curious attitude so that you can see clearly what is happening. You
want to be able to make the most skillful response you can in any given
situation. The only way to know if it is time to shift gears is to be very
aware of how your opponents see you. In large part, their perception of
you drives what you should be doing. Don’t simply act or react on autopi-
lot. Take the time to consider all options before deciding what to do.
   I don’t know if pressure played a role, but I want to bring it up just in
case it did. Some people feel a certain pressure to perform in a certain
way when they know the cameras are on them. It’s important to resist
the pressure and stick to optimal play. Understand that no matter what is
going on, you have the power to choose your response.
   Finally, sometimes losing a big pot inspires us to “chase” our losses. Be
wary of this response. If you start to take unnecessary risks just to get
your stack back to where it was, it can lead to substantial losses.
   Switching gears is all about being aware of yourself and your oppo-
nents as well as thinking about the best possible response you can have in
any given situation. Try to make it a matter of policy to take a few mo-
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

ments to review these points any time you win or lose a large pot. This
will help you make a conscious decision about whether or not it is time to
change gears.
   I asked Jonathan to chime in with his thoughts on your question since
he is a master MTT strategist. He said:

      It is vitally important that you are aware of your image. Many
      players naturally have a tight image that allows them to run
      normally optimistic bluffs when they are unknown to their op-
      ponents. However, if you are clearly involved in every pot,
      your opponents will eventually catch onto this and adjust. If
      you have been involved in many pots in the recent past with-
      out showing down many hands, you should usually tighten up.
      You must be aware of what your opponents think about you.

    It is important that you recognize that it is quite easy to lose a signifi-
cant stack in a tournament. If you are the chip leader, but you only have
75 big blinds, it is reasonable likely that you can lose three 25 big blind
pots in a row if you pick up a string of reasonable hands. You must accept
that this is part of tournament poker.
    A common occurrence for most world-class players is to double up in
the first eight or so levels by winning small pots, profiting perhaps 100 big
blinds, then losing a few 20 big blind all-ins to be out a few levels later. As
the blinds increase, it becomes much easier to get all-in and experience
variance in full force. Sometimes it simply doesn’t work out for you.
```

## PDF page 248

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/Peak%20Poker%20Performance.pdf#page=248)

```text
                                                        Readers’ Questions

is to learn that we have the freedom to choose our response no matter
what situation we find ourselves in. The most elegant proponent of this
idea came from Victor Frankl in his book Man’s Search for Meaning. He
was interned in a concentration camp during WWII, where he formulated
a theory called logotherapy. He said that no matter what happens to us,
we always have the freedom to choose our response.
    We might have the erroneous idea that tilt is a given when we lose a
big pot or take a bad beat. We tend to do whatever it is that we have ha-
bitually done in the past, so if you are used to tilting that response is
probably queued up and ready to go. Frankl says that with practice we
can learn to widen the gap between the stimulus (which is the annoying
event like a bad beat) and our response. We don’t have to react instanta-
neously. We can widen the gap between the stimulus and response to
give ourselves time to come up with a more optimal response.
    Try practicing this idea with mundane things in everyday life that irri-
tate you. Notice what your reaction is when something unpleasant hap-
pens to you away from the table. Do you react sub-optimally? If you do,
see if you can come up with a better response and do that instead. Try to
get a little better with each little annoyance. Over time you’ll get used to
dealing with irritants with equanimity and, hopefully, this will extend to
dealing with irritants at the table.
    When something does comes up at the table, consciously ask yourself,
“Do I need to get triggered by this?” then “Is there anything I can do
about this?” If it is something within your control, take care of it. If it is
not, let it go. You always want to be mindful of what the best possible
response is in each moment. Train yourself to go through this process and
you’ll probably find yourself tilting a whole lot less.
```
